cap: Step 1 of 9 — linear falloff, written with d. With “linear”, the falloff graph is a straight line inside the band. We write falloff with d, the distance from C to the pixel, one move per line. The numbers column checks every line with a pixel on the circle edge (d = 0.25).
known: shader radius 0.25, band 0.10, the rule “linear” found here falloff as a formula of d
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: a pixel on the circle edge, d = 0.251sd: how far the pixel is past the circle edge (sd rule)sd = d − 0.250.25 − 0.25 = 02t: how far sd is through the band (Lesson 9.3)t = (sd − (−0.10)) ÷ (0.10 − (−0.10))(0 − (−0.10)) ÷ (0.10 − (−0.10))3the bottom: 0.10 − (−0.10) is 0.10 + 0.10t = (sd − (−0.10)) ÷ 0.200.10 + 0.10 = 0.204the top: “− (−0.10)” is “+ 0.10”t = (sd + 0.10) ÷ 0.200 + 0.10 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.55put in the sd rule from line 1t = (d − 0.25 + 0.10) ÷ 0.200.25 − 0.25 = 0 0 + 0.10 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.56add the two numbers: −0.25 + 0.10 = −0.15t = (d − 0.15) ÷ 0.200.25 − 0.15 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.57linear falloff is 1 − t (Lesson 9.3)falloff = 1 − t1 − 0.5 = 0.58put in t from line 6falloff = 1 − (d − 0.15) ÷ 0.200.25 − 0.15 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.5 1 − 0.5 = 0.59write 1 as 0.20 ÷ 0.20, so both parts are “something ÷ 0.20”falloff = (0.20 − (d − 0.15)) ÷ 0.200.25 − 0.15 = 0.10 0.20 − 0.10 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.510remove the inner brackets: the minus in front flips both signs inside: − (d − 0.15) = − d + 0.15falloff = (0.20 − d + 0.15) ÷ 0.200.20 − 0.25 = −0.05 −0.05 + 0.15 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.511add the two numbers: 0.20 + 0.15 = 0.35falloff = (0.35 − d) ÷ 0.200.35 − 0.25 = 0.10 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.5

cap: Step 2 of 9 — the push, written with d. The push is dispLen × falloff. We put the falloff formula of step 1 into it.
known: shader dispLen 0.10 found here the push as a formula of d
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: the same pixel, d = 0.251the push is dispLen × falloff, with dispLen = 0.10push = 0.10 × fallofffalloff = 0.5 (step 1) 0.10 × 0.5 = 0.052put in the falloff formula (step 1)push = 0.10 × (0.35 − d) ÷ 0.200.35 − 0.25 = 0.10 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.01 0.01 ÷ 0.20 = 0.053do the division of the two numbers first (× and ÷ can go in any order): 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.5push = 0.5 × (0.35 − d)0.35 − 0.25 = 0.10 0.5 × 0.10 = 0.054multiply each part of the bracket by 0.5: 0.5 × 0.35 = 0.175, and 0.5 × dpush = 0.175 − 0.5 × d0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 0.175 − 0.125 = 0.05
result: New: push formula push = 0.175 − 0.5 × d from step 2 — the pixel on the circle edge gets half of 0.10.

cap: Step 3 of 9 — pick a point R of the white line. We pick the point of the white line that is 0.20 from C, so that the numbers stay short. d_read is the distance from C to R. It is the same length formula as d, used for the point R instead of for a pixel.
known: our choice the white line x = 0.65, and d_read = 0.20 found here R.y = 0.368
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: R, 0.20 from C1the distance from C to R, squared (length formula, used for R): R is 0.15 right of C0.15² + (0.50 − R.y)² = d_read²0.15 × 0.15 = 0.0225 0.20 × 0.20 = 0.042take 0.15² away from both sides(0.50 − R.y)² = d_read² − 0.15²0.04 − 0.0225 = 0.01753take the square root of both sides0.50 − R.y = √(d_read² − 0.15²)√0.0175 = 0.1324move R.y to one side and the number to the other sideR.y = 0.50 − √(d_read² − 0.15²)0.50 − 0.132 = 0.3685check with the length formula of the chain, used for Rd_read = √((R.x − 0.50)² + (R.y − 0.50)²)0.65 − 0.50 = 0.15 0.368 − 0.50 = −0.132 0.15 × 0.15 = 0.0225 (−0.132) × (−0.132) = 0.017424 0.0225 + 0.017424 = 0.039924 √0.039924 = 0.20
result: R = (0.65, 0.368), and d_read = 0.20. (The lesson writes R.y = 0.367712: the same point with 6 decimals.)

cap: Step 4 of 9 — the ray rule. The push of a pixel points straight at C (in the chain, dir = p ÷ d points away from C, and readUv = uv − dir × push goes back toward C). So the pixel S that shows R lies on the violet ray from C through R, and S is farther from C than R by exactly the push of S. Three rulers beside the ray measure the three lengths. They are drawn beside the ray, not on it, so that they do not cover the ray and the push arrow.
known: our choice R, d_read = 0.20 found here the ray rule, true for every pixel and every falloff rule
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: R and S (the numbers of S come from step 6; here they only check the rule)1read the three rulers beside the violet ray: the blue ruler (C to R) and the teal ruler (R to S) together are as long as the yellow ruler (C to S)d_read + push = d0.20 + 0.05 = 0.252take the push away from both sidesd_read = d − push0.25 − 0.05 = 0.20
result: New: ray rule d_read = d − push from step 4 — for every pixel: its read point is closer to C by its push.

cap: Step 5 of 9 — put the push formula into the ray rule. The ray rule still contains the word “push”. The push formula of step 2 says what the push is for a pixel at distance d. We put it in — like inlining a variable in code — and then tidy up, one move per line.
known: found here d_read as a formula of d: where a pixel at distance d reads
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: S: d = 0.251start from the ray rule (step 4)d_read = d − push0.25 − 0.05 = 0.202put in the push formula (step 2)d_read = d − (0.175 − 0.5 × d)0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 0.175 − 0.125 = 0.05 0.25 − 0.05 = 0.203remove the brackets: the minus in front flips both signs inside: − (0.175 − 0.5 × d) = − 0.175 + 0.5 × dd_read = d − 0.175 + 0.5 × d0.25 − 0.175 = 0.075 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 0.075 + 0.125 = 0.204put the two d’s together: d + 0.5 × d = 1.5 × dd_read = 1.5 × d − 0.1751.5 × 0.25 = 0.375 0.375 − 0.175 = 0.20
result: New: read-distance formula d_read = 1.5 × d − 0.175 from step 5 — where a pixel at distance d reads (inside the band).

cap: Step 6 of 9 — turn it around: d from d_read. We know d_read, because we chose R. We look for d, the distance of the pixel that shows R. So we move everything except d to the other side, one move per line. The graph is not a part of the wallpaper or the output. It shows one ray from C: across, where a pixel is (its distance d); up, where the pixel reads (the distance d_read of its read point). The strip under the graph draws the same ray, laid flat.
known: our choice d_read = 0.20 looked for d found here d = 0.25
table: #What we do (one move per line)With lettersWith numbers: R: d_read = 0.20 — here we find d1start from the read-distance formula (step 5)d_read = 1.5 × d − 0.175put in d_read = 0.20: 0.20 = 1.5 × d − 0.1752add 0.175 to both sides: on the right, − 0.175 + 0.175 = 0d_read + 0.175 = 1.5 × d0.20 + 0.175 = 0.375 0.375 = 1.5 × d3divide both sides by 1.5: on the right, 1.5 × d ÷ 1.5 = d(d_read + 0.175) ÷ 1.5 = d0.375 ÷ 1.5 = 0.25 0.25 = d4swap the two sidesd = (d_read + 0.175) ÷ 1.5d = 0.25
result: New: pixel-distance formula d = (d_read + 0.175) ÷ 1.5 from step 6 — S, the pixel that shows R, is 0.25 from C: on the circle edge.

cap: Step 7 of 9 — the stretch rule. S lies on the violet ray from C through R, d ÷ d_read times as far from C. The triangle from C to S is the triangle from C to R, enlarged d ÷ d_read times. So the sideways offset from C is enlarged by the same number.
known: known R = (0.65, 0.368), d_read = 0.20, d = 0.25 looked for S found here S = (0.6875, 0.335)

cap: Step 8 of 9 — put the pixel-distance formula into the stretch rule. The stretch rule still contains d. The pixel-distance formula of step 6 gives d from d_read. We put it in and tidy up, one move per line. The numbers column puts d_read = 0.20 into every line: the value stays 0.6875 on every line, so no move changed the result.
known: found here the x of the pixel that shows a point of the white line, from its distance d_read alone: no d, no trying

result: New: curve formula x = 0.60 + 0.0175 ÷ d_read from step 8 — valid inside the band: d_read from 0.15 (the peak) to 0.35 (P). Above P the push is 0, and the curve is the white line itself. The yellow dots are made by this formula from the white dots.

cap: Step 9 of 9 — compare with a straight line. The gray line is the straight line through P and the peak: the two ends of the bent part of the curve. Here we build its formula from two points of the curve formula, on this screen. Then we measure the gap between the curve and the gray line at S. A straight line has the form x = (a fixed number) + (a fixed number) × y. The curve formula divides by d_read, and d_read contains a square root, so the curve cannot have that form.
known: known the curve formula (step 8), S (step 7) found here the gray line, and the gap at S

The curve formula gives the x of its pixel: 0.65. So P gets no push; P shows itselfx = 0.60 + 0.0175 ÷ d_read0.0175 ÷ 0.35 = 0.05 0.60 + 0.05 = 0.652P.y: the point of the white line 0.35 from C (length formula, as in step 3)P.y = 0.50 − √(0.35² − 0.15²)0.35 × 0.35 = 0.1225 0.15 × 0.15 = 0.0225 0.1225 − 0.0225 = 0.10 √0.10 = 0.316 0.50 − 0.316 = 0.1843the peak shows the point (0.65, 0.50) of the white line: it is 0.15 from C, so d_read = 0.15. The curve formula againx = 0.60 + 0.0175 ÷ d_read0.0175 ÷ 0.15 = 0.117 0.60 + 0.117 = 0.717 the peak = (0.717, 0.50)4the gray line: the straight line through P and the peak — a lerp (Chapter 5): x moves by the same amount for every step of yx = P.x + (y − P.y) ÷ (peak.y − P.y) × (peak.x − P.x)0.50 − 0.184 = 0.316 0.717 − 0.65 = 0.0675do the division of the two fixed numbers first (× and ÷ can go in any order): (peak.x − P.x) ÷ (peak.y − P.y)x = 0.65 + (y − 0.184) × 0.2120.067 ÷ 0.316 = 0.2126multiply the bracket out: (y − 0.184) × 0.212 = 0.212 × y − 0.184 × 0.212x = 0.65 − 0.184 × 0.212 + 0.212 × y0.184 × 0.212 = 0.0397subtract the two fixed numbersx = 0.611 + 0.212 × y0.65 − 0.039 = 0.6118the gray line on the row of S, y = 0.335x = 0.611 + 0.212 × 0.3350.212 × 0.335 = 0.071 0.611 + 0.071 = 0.6829the gap at S: the curve minus the gray line (the red segment)gap = S.x − gray-line x0.6875 − 0.682 = 0.0055
result: The gray line: x = 0.611 + 0.212 × y — only “fixed + fixed × y”. The curve: x = 0.60 + 0.0175 ÷ d_read — “÷ d_read”, and d_read has a square root inside. At S the curve is 0.0055 to the right of the gray line (the thick red segment). The lesson writes the gray line with 6 decimals: x = 0.611257 + 0.210819 × y. With 3 decimals the second number is 0.212, not 0.211, because 0.066667 was rounded to 0.067 before the division.
